why_angle: The cited kit comparison gives solar-input windows for the EcoFlow, Jackery, Apex 200 and Anker stations. It gives none for the ALLPOWERS R3500 or BLUETTI Elite 300 and no voltage window for the Apex 300, and it never checks a kit's own panel Voc against those windows. This page shows that the R3500 kits can put two SP039 panels or three SP037 panels in series under the 150 V limit, while the BLUETTI inputs stop at 60 V. That answers the open caveat 'provided the station supports them' about growing a kit to 800–1,200 W of panels.

What the differences mean

Dealectric does not test these units. Every figure here comes from the maker's store, the maker's manual or a named reviewer, read on 2026-11-17. Refill times are arithmetic at the panels' rated output (battery Wh ÷ panel W). Real output in sun is lower.

  • R3500 + SP039: $1,753.93 through our link (store $1,993.10) ÷ 3,168 Wh = $0.55 per Wh. 3,168 ÷ 600 W = 5.3 h of full sun.
  • R3500 + SP037: $1,586.73 through our link (store $1,803.10) ÷ 3,168 Wh = $0.50 per Wh. 3,168 ÷ 400 W = 7.9 h.
  • Elite 300 + 2 × 200 W: $1,614.05 through our link (store $1,699.00) ÷ 3,014.4 Wh = $0.54 per Wh. 3,014.4 ÷ 400 W = 7.5 h. On BLUETTI's store it costs $298 less than the same parts bought separately.
  • Apex 300 + 2 × 200 W: $2,089.05 through our link (store $2,199.00) ÷ 2,764.8 Wh = $0.76 per Wh. 2,764.8 ÷ 400 W = 6.9 h.
  • Anker SOLIX F3000 + 400 W: 3,072 ÷ 400 W = 7.7 h.
  • Grow either R3500 kit to 1,200 W (one more SP039, or two more SP037): 3,168 ÷ 1,200 W = 2.6 h.

Size line: batteries from 2,400 to 3,600 Wh (3,000 Wh ± 20%). BLUETTI Elite 400 kits (3,840 Wh) and bundles with expansion batteries fall outside it. BLUETTI Apex 200 kits (2,560 Wh) fall inside it and, like the Apex 300, ship late January 2027. EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra and Jackery HomePower 3000 kits also fall inside the line, but neither maker's US store showed a kit price on 2026-11-17, so they are left out of the table.

How much solar each kit can grow to

Panels wired in series add their voltages. The string's open-circuit voltage (Voc) has to stay under the station's input ceiling. Cold weather raises Voc, so leave some headroom. After that, the input's amp and watt limits cap what a string can deliver.

  • ALLPOWERS R3500: one solar input rated 12–150 V, 40 A, 2,000 W. The R3500 manual shows panels wired in series and says to keep panel output within 150 V. The SP039 has a Voc of 52.8 V (SP039 manual), so two in series make 105.6 V and 1,200 W rated. A third would reach 158.4 V, over the ceiling. The SP037 has a Voc of 45.3 V (SP037 manual), so three in series make 135.9 V, about 10% under the ceiling. A fourth would reach 181.2 V.
  • BLUETTI Elite 300: 12–60 V, 22 A, 1,200 W (StorageReview). Each string of added panels has to stay under 60 V Voc, so long series strings of large panels won't work on it.
  • BLUETTI Apex 300: two inputs, each rated 1,200 W, 12–60 V, 20 A (StorageReview). 1,200 W ÷ 20 A = 60 V, the very top of the window, so an input reaches its full 1,200 W only with a string working at 60 V. BLUETTI's 4,000 W solar figure requires its separate SolarX 4K controller.
  • Anker SOLIX F3000: a High-PV input rated 11–165 V, 17 A, 1,600 W and a Low-PV input rated 11–60 V, 17 A, 800 W (Anker). The 2,400 W total needs both inputs in use. The kit's single 400 W panel fills one.

Not recommended

BLUETTI Apex 300 + 2 × 500 W: $3,134.05 through our link (store $3,299.00), which is $1.13 per Wh (3,134.05 ÷ 2,764.8). On 2026-11-17 BLUETTI's store charged $102 more for this kit than for the station and the two panels bought separately, and the kit is a pre-order that ships late January 2027. Its 2.8 h refill (2,764.8 ÷ 1,000 W) is the fastest in this table. If you want that much solar on an Apex 300, buy the parts separately.
